description: We are a team of five students from Düzce University, Türkiye. We’re interested in space, data and building cool things on the web. Between us we have skills in coding, data analysis, design and presentation. We’re excited to learn, have fun and build something useful over the weekend. Our team is complete, so we’re not looking for new members right now.
summary:
Martian Map is a walk planner for the first astronauts who will explore Mars on foot. Planning one surface walk today means checking many separate sources: terrain, slope, weather, Sun angle and radiation. We bring them together on one screen.

The user clicks any two points on the map. The app returns three routes: the fastest, the safest and an alternative. They are computed in the browser from a 1 m USGS elevation model. Ground steeper than 25° is treated as impassable, walking speed comes from Tobler's hiking function adjusted for a pressure suit, and the safest route avoids steep slopes and radio shadow. Each route shows its duration, oxygen use (with a 25% reserve kept), radiation dose, maximum slope and minutes without contact.

Our study area is Gale crater, at the clay-to-sulfate transition on Mount Sharp that Curiosity crossed between 2019 and 2023. This is where Mars changed from a wetter world to a drier one. Each stop shows real Curiosity photos and a short science note.

The app has five main parts:

Layered map: HiRISE imagery, THEMIS infrared, geology, slope, radio shadow and shelters.
EVA window: the hours when the walk is allowed, from JPL Horizons Sun angles and Curiosity REMS temperatures.
3D view: a fly-over of each route on the real terrain.
HUD mode: an astronaut visor that shows the next stop and the remaining oxygen and dose, and raises alerts.
Storm replay: the real 20 May 2024 solar storm. The HUD guides the astronaut to the nearest shelter.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Martian Map plans a safe astronaut walk (EVA) in Gale crater, at the clay-to-sulfate transition on Mount Sharp that Curiosity crossed between 2019 and 2023.

The user picks a start and a destination anywhere on the map. The start defaults to the habitat, and the 5 terrain shelters are offered as suggestions. The app computes the routes in the browser with an A* search on a heightmap built from the 1 m USGS elevation model:

  • Ground steeper than 25° is impassable.
  • Walking speed follows Tobler's hiking function, reduced for a pressure suit.
  • The fastest route minimises time.
  • The safest route also penalises steep slopes and radio shadow, the places where the habitat antenna cannot reach the astronaut.
  • A third, alternative route takes a different path.

Each route shows its distance, duration, oxygen use (keeping a 25% reserve), radiation dose, maximum slope and minutes without contact. It also has an elevation profile and a 3D fly-over on the real terrain.

The rest of the app:

  • Layered map: HiRISE imagery, THEMIS day and night infrared, geology, slope, roughness, radio shadow and shelters.
  • Stop cards: real Curiosity photos with a short science note.
  • EVA window: the hours when a walk is allowed, from JPL Horizons Sun angles and Curiosity REMS temperatures.
  • HUD mode: an astronaut visor that shows the next stop, the remaining oxygen and dose, and alerts. It replays two scenarios: the real 20 May 2024 solar storm (NASA DONKI, Curiosity RAD), during which the astronaut is guided to the nearest shelter, and a dust devil to step aside from.

What benefits does it have?

  • It puts terrain, weather, Sun, radiation and communication data on one screen, where today they would be checked one by one.
  • A planner gets a full, checkable plan in seconds. Every number has a stated source and assumption.
  • Fastest and safest routes appear side by side, so the trade-off is visible.
  • The astronaut gets a simple visor view during the walk, with alerts and a way to shelter.

What is the intended impact?

We want to show how future crewed Mars missions, and Artemis-style EVAs on the Moon, could plan surface walks with open data. Safety comes first and the science stays in view. The same method works for any site with an elevation model and orbital imagery. The project also helps the public understand what walking on Mars would really involve.

What tools, languages, hardware and software did you use?

  • Data pipeline: Python 3.11 with rasterio, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image, pyproj, Pillow, Matplotlib and requests, plus the GDAL command-line tools.
  • Frontend: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript (ES modules, no build step), Leaflet with a Mars-radius map projection, Chart.js and three.js.
  • Hosting: GitHub Pages; the team worked in Git and GitHub.
  • Data: USGS 1 m DEM, NASA Mars Trek (HiRISE, THEMIS), Curiosity raw images, traverse and REMS, JPL Horizons, NASA DONKI, USGS geologic map.
  • Hardware: our own laptops; the app runs in any modern browser.

How is the project creative?

  • It works like a navigation app for Mars: click a point and get a route, with costs for oxygen, radiation and radio contact.
  • The routes are drawn in a 3D view of the real terrain, where the astronaut's walk is animated.
  • A HUD simulates an astronaut's visor and replays a real solar storm from 2024.
  • Real Curiosity photos are placed exactly where they were taken, so every stop tells the clay-to-sulfate story.

What factors did the team consider?

  • Safety: every threshold (slope, oxygen reserve, Sun elevation, temperature, radiation) lives in one configuration file and is documented with its source.
  • Honesty: the oxygen and dose models are simplified, and the assumptions are listed openly. THEMIS infrared is coarse (about 100 m per pixel), so we show it only as an information layer and do not use it for routing.
  • Real data only: no invented terrain; photos are shown by URL with NASA/JPL-Caltech credit.
  • Reliability: data is fetched ahead of time, so there are no API keys or calls in the browser. If a data file is missing, the app still opens.
  • Usability and performance: it runs on a laptop with no installation, and the 3D view loads only when it is opened.
  • Teamwork: the code is split into modules, and every dataset has one owner, so five people could work in parallel.
